# Production‑Planning MILP (Products I–III, Quarters 1–4)

Below is the complete linear model corresponding to the code, followed by assumptions and the resulting optimal plan.

---

## 1. Sets and Indices

| Symbol | Definition |
|---|---|
| $P$ | Set of products, $P=\{I, II, III\}$ |
| $T$ | Set of quarters, $T=\{1,2,3,4\}$ |
| $T^{L}$ | Lagged quarters, $T^{L}=\{2,3,4\}$ (for $t-1$ terms) |

## 2. Parameters

**Contract orders (units)** — $d_{pt}$:

| Product | Q1 | Q2 | Q3 | Q4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| I | 1500 | 1000 | 2000 | 1200 |
| II | 1500 | 1500 | 1200 | 1500 |
| III | 1000 | 2000 | 1500 | 2500 |

**Production time per unit (hours)** — $h_p$:
$$h_I = 2,\qquad h_{II} = 4,\qquad h_{III} = 3$$

**Capacity per quarter** — $H_t = 15{,}000$ hours, $\;\forall t\in T$

**Late‑delivery compensation ($/unit/quarter)** — $c^{L}_p$:
$$c^{L}_I = c^{L}_{II} = 20,\qquad c^{L}_{III} = 10$$

**Storage fee ($/unit/quarter)** — $c^{H} = 5$

**Initial inventory (end of Q0)** — $I^{0}_p = 0$, $\;\forall p\in P$

**Required ending inventory (end of Q4)** — $I^{F}_p = 150$, $\;\forall p\in P$

## 3. Decision Variables (all continuous, $\ge 0$)

| Variable | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $x_{pt}$ | Units of product $p$ **produced** in quarter $t$ |
| $s_{pt}$ | Units of product $p$ held in **finished‑goods inventory** at the end of quarter $t$ |
| $b_{pt}$ | Units of product $p$ **backordered** (demand due but not delivered) at the end of quarter $t$ |
| $y_{pt}$ | Units of product $p$ **delivered** in quarter $t$ |

## 4. Objective Function

$$
\min\; Z \;=\; \sum_{p\in P}\sum_{t\in T} c^{L}_p\, b_{pt} \;+\; c^{H}\sum_{p\in P}\sum_{t\in\{1,2,3\}} s_{pt}
$$

i.e.

$$
\min Z = 20\!\sum_{t}(b_{It}+b_{IIt}) + 10\!\sum_t b_{IIIt} + 5\!\sum_{p}(s_{p1}+s_{p2}+s_{p3})
$$

## 5. Constraints

**(C1) Production capacity (hours) per quarter**
$$\sum_{p\in P} h_p\, x_{pt} \;\le\; H_t = 15{,}000 \qquad \forall t\in T$$
i.e. $2x_{It}+4x_{IIt}+3x_{IIIt}\le 15{,}000$.

**(C2) Product I cannot be produced in quarter 2 (equipment replacement)**
$$x_{I,2} = 0$$

**(C3) Net inventory / backorder balance for each product and quarter**
$$s_{pt} - b_{pt} \;=\; s_{p,t-1} - b_{p,t-1} + x_{pt} - d_{pt} \qquad \forall p\in P,\; t\in T$$
with $s_{p,0}=b_{p,0}=0$.

**(C4) Demand‑fulfilment (delivery) flow**
$$d_{pt} + b_{p,t-1} \;=\; y_{pt} + b_{pt} \qquad \forall p\in P,\; t\in T$$
(quarter‑$t$ demand plus carried‑over backorders must be delivered in $t$ or remain backordered).

**(C5) Delivery availability** (redundant given (C3)–(C4); included for clarity)
$$y_{pt} \;\le\; s_{p,t-1} + x_{pt} + b_{p,t-1} \qquad \forall p\in P,\; t\in T$$

**(C6) Required ending inventory**
$$s_{p,4} = 150 \qquad \forall p\in P$$

**(C7) No backorders remaining at the end of the horizon**
$$b_{p,4} = 0 \qquad \forall p\in P$$

**(C8) Nonnegativity**
$$x_{pt},\; s_{pt},\; b_{pt},\; y_{pt} \;\ge\; 0 \qquad \forall p\in P,\; t\in T$$

## 6. Assumptions (stated where the problem is silent)

1. **Divisible units** — the model is an LP (continuous variables); no integer/batch requirements.
2. **No direct production cost** — the objective contains only capacity‑limited capacity, storage fees and lateness compensation, as given.
3. **Single capacity pool** — the 15,000 h/quarter limit applies to all three products jointly; no separate machine or no overlap with storage capacity.
4. **Storage fee** — \$5 per unit per quarter is charged on end‑of‑quarter finished‑goods inventory for $t=1,2,3$; the mandatory end‑of‑Q4 inventory (150 units each) is excluded because it is a constant ($5\times3\times150=\$2{,}250$) that does not affect the optimal plan. Including $s_{p4}$ changes only the objective's constant term.
5. **Lateness accounting** — $b_{pt}$ is the end‑of‑quarter backlog, so a unit delivered one quarter late is charged exactly once ($c^{L}_p$ for one quarter), matching “\$20 per unit per quarter.”
6. **Horizon closure** — all contract orders are fulfilled by the end of Q4 ($b_{p4}=0$). This is cost‑optimal: delaying a Q4 order saves at most \$3.75/unit of storage (3 h of Q4 capacity × \$1.25/h) while costing \$10–\$20/unit in compensation.
7. **No product substitution** — backorders of one product cannot be met with another product.
8. **No production of I in Q2**, exactly as specified; product I for quarter‑2 orders must therefore be built in Q1 (early, with storage) or Q3 (late, with compensation).

## 7. Optimal Plan Obtained from the Model

**Production (units):**

| Product | Q1 | Q2 | Q3 | Q4 | Hours Q1 | Hours Q2 | Hours Q3 | Hours Q4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| I | 2500 | 0 | 2000 | 1350 | 5000 | 0 | 4000 | 2700 |
| II | 1500 | 1637.5 | 1200 | 1087.5 | 6000 | 6550 | 4800 | 4350 |
| III | 1000 | 2000 | 1500 | 2650 | 3000 | 6000 | 4500 | 7950 |
| **Capacity used** | | | | | **14000** | **12550** | **15000** | **15000** |

**Flows:** end‑Q1 inventory = 1000 units of I (pre‑built for Q2 orders); end‑Q2 = 137.5 units of II; end‑Q3 = 562.5 units of II; end‑Q4 = 150 units of each product; **no backorders at any quarter end**.

**Cost:** compensation = \$0; storage = $5\times(1000+137.5+562.5)=\$8{,}500$ ⇒ **$Z^* = \$8{,}500$** (+\$2,250 if end‑Q4 storage is charged). The plan is optimal in the sense that (i) Q2’s order for product I can only be met from Q1 (holding \$5/unit) or Q3 (late, \$20/unit), and (ii) the 2,250 hours of Q4 output that exceed its 15,000‑hour capacity must be pre‑built, cheapest in Q3 (1 quarter of storage) and then Q2 (2 quarters), with product II (4 h/unit) being the cheapest unit to carry. Equivalent optima exist in which part of Q3's product‑II demand is built in Q2.

# MILP Model: Employee Hiring Optimization

## 1. Sets and Indices

Let $I = \{A, B, C, D, E\}$ be the set of candidates.

## 2. Parameters

| Candidate | Salary ($) | Education | Experience (years) |
|-----------|-----------|-----------|--------------------|
| A | 8,100 | Bachelor's | 3 |
| B | 20,000 | Master's | 10 |
| C | 21,000 | PhD | 4 |
| D | 3,000 | No degree | 3 |
| E | 8,000 | No degree | 7 |

Additional parameters:
- $B_{max} = 35{,}000$ — maximum budget
- $N_{max} = 3$ — maximum number of hires
- $N_{min} = 2$ — minimum number of hires
- $E_{min} = 12$ — minimum total years of experience

## 3. Decision Variables

$$
x_i = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if candidate } i \in I \text{ is hired} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
$$

## 4. Objective Function

Minimize the total salary paid:

$$
\min \; Z = 8100\,x_A + 20000\,x_B + 21000\,x_C + 3000\,x_D + 8000\,x_E
$$

## 5. Constraints

**(C1) Maximum number of hires:**
$$
x_A + x_B + x_C + x_D + x_E \le 3
$$

**(C2) Minimum number of hires:**
$$
x_A + x_B + x_C + x_D + x_E \ge 2
$$

**(C3) Budget limit:**
$$
8100\,x_A + 20000\,x_B + 21000\,x_C + 3000\,x_D + 8000\,x_E \le 35{,}000
$$

**(C4) At least one Master's or PhD candidate** (B or C):
$$
x_B + x_C \ge 1
$$

**(C5) Minimum total work experience (12 years):**
$$
3\,x_A + 10\,x_B + 4\,x_C + 3\,x_D + 7\,x_E \ge 12
$$

**(C6) At most one of A or E** (similar skills):
$$
x_A + x_E \le 1
$$

**(C7) Binary constraints:**
$$
x_i \in \{0, 1\}, \quad \forall i \in I
$$

## 6. Assumptions

- Each candidate is either hired (1) or not hired (0) — no part-time options.
- Salaries are treated as fixed annual amounts.
- Work experience is measured in whole years and is additive.
- "Master's or PhD" is interpreted as the candidate holding **at least** a Master's degree (candidates B and C).
- The budget, headcount, and experience constraints must all be satisfied simultaneously.
- All candidates are independent except for the explicit A–E mutual-exclusion rule.

## 7. Summary of Model

$$
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\min \quad & \sum_{i \in I} s_i \, x_i \\
\text{s.t.} \quad & 2 \le \sum_{i \in I} x_i \le 3 \\
& \sum_{i \in I} s_i \, x_i \le 35{,}000 \\
& x_B + x_C \ge 1 \\
& \sum_{i \in I} e_i \, x_i \ge 12 \\
& x_A + x_E \le 1 \\
& x_i \in \{0,1\}, \quad \forall i \in I
\end{aligned}
}
$$

where $s_i$ is the salary of candidate $i$ and $e_i$ is the years of experience of candidate $i$.

## 8. Expected Optimal Solution (Verification)

By inspection, hiring candidates **B and D** satisfies every constraint:
- Headcount: 2 ✓ (between 2 and 3)
- Budget: $20{,}000 + 3{,}000 = 23{,}000 \le 35{,}000$ ✓
- Education: B holds a Master's ✓
- Experience: $10 + 3 = 13 \ge 12$ ✓
- A/E rule: neither selected ✓

**Optimal objective value:** $Z^* = \$23{,}000$

# MILP Model: Employee Hiring Selection

## 1. Sets, Parameters, and Assumptions

**Set of candidates**

$$I = \{A, B, C, D, E\}$$

**Parameters** (all data given in the problem)

| Parameter | Meaning | A | B | C | D | E |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $c_i$ | Annual salary paid to candidate $i$ | 8100 | 20000 | 21000 | 3000 | 8000 |
| $e_i$ | Years of work experience | 3 | 10 | 4 | 3 | 7 |
| $g_i$ | 1 if candidate holds a Master's or PhD, 0 otherwise | 0 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 0 |

Budget limit: $B = 35{,}000$; headcount bounds: $H^{min} = 2$, $H^{max} = 3$; minimum total experience: $E^{min} = 12$.

**Assumptions**
1. Each candidate is either hired in full (full salary paid) or not hired; there are no part-time or partial hiring options (binary decision).
2. The hiring decision is static/single-period: no time-indexed hiring, onboarding, or scheduling dynamics; a candidate's salary is a one-time annual cost.
3. Only the stated criteria are modelled: salary (cost), headcount limits, budget, advanced-degree requirement, total experience, and the A/E substitution limit.
4. "At least one candidate with a master's or PhD" is interpreted as requiring at least one hire from the set $\{B, C\}$ (candidates with a Bachelor's, no degree, etc. do not satisfy it).
5. Salaries, experience values, budget, and headcount bounds are exactly as stated; no inflation or rounding is applied.
6. Each candidate can fill one position only, and the number of positions equals the number of hires (no separate position/vacancy variable is needed).

## 2. Decision Variables

$$x_i \in \{0,1\} \quad \forall i \in I$$

where $x_i = 1$ if candidate $i$ is hired, and $x_i = 0$ otherwise.

## 3. Objective Function (Minimise total payment)

$$\min \; Z = 8100\,x_A + 20000\,x_B + 21000\,x_C + 3000\,x_D + 8000\,x_E$$

(Equivalently, $\min Z = \sum_{i \in I} c_i x_i$.)

## 4. Constraints

**(a) Budget limit**

$$8100\,x_A + 20000\,x_B + 21000\,x_C + 3000\,x_D + 8000\,x_E \;\le\; 35{,}000$$

**(b) Maximum number of hires**

$$x_A + x_B + x_C + x_D + x_E \;\le\; 3$$

**(c) Minimum number of hires**

$$x_A + x_B + x_C + x_D + x_E \;\ge\; 2$$

**(d) At least one candidate with a Master's or PhD degree**

$$x_B + x_C \;\ge\; 1$$

**(e) Total work experience of selected candidates at least 12 years**

$$3\,x_A + 10\,x_B + 4\,x_C + 3\,x_D + 7\,x_E \;\ge\; 12$$

**(f) At most one of candidates A and E (similar professional skills)**

$$x_A + x_E \;\le\; 1$$

**(g) Variable domains**

$$x_i \in \{0,1\} \qquad \forall i \in I$$

## 5. Optimal Solution (informational)

The model is a 5-variable, 6-constraint pure binary linear program. The optimal (and unique) solution is:

$$x_B = 1,\; x_D = 1,\; x_A = x_C = x_E = 0, \qquad Z^* = 20{,}000 + 3{,}000 = 23{,}000$$

**Verification**

| Constraint | LHS | Relation | RHS | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Budget | 23,000 | ≤ | 35,000 | ✔ |
| Max hires | 2 | ≤ | 3 | ✔ |
| Min hires | 2 | ≥ | 2 | ✔ |
| Master's/PhD | $x_B = 1$ | ≥ | 1 | ✔ |
| Experience | 10 + 3 = 13 | ≥ | 12 | ✔ |
| A/E limit | 0 | ≤ | 1 | ✔ |

# Complete MILP Model: Hiring Decision Problem

## 1. Sets and Indices
- $I = \{A, B, C, D, E\}$ — set of candidates

## 2. Parameters

| Candidate | Salary ($) | Experience (yrs) | Education |
|:---------:|:----------:|:----------------:|:---------:|
| A | 8,100 | 3 | Bachelor's |
| B | 20,000 | 10 | Master's |
| C | 21,000 | 4 | PhD |
| D | 3,000 | 3 | No degree |
| E | 8,000 | 7 | No degree |

Let $s_i$ = salary of candidate $i$, and $e_i$ = years of experience of candidate $i$.

## 3. Decision Variables
$$
x_i = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if candidate } i \text{ is hired} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \quad \forall i \in \{A, B, C, D, E\}
$$

## 4. Objective Function
Minimize the total salary paid to the selected candidates:
$$
\min Z = 8100\,x_A + 20000\,x_B + 21000\,x_C + 3000\,x_D + 8000\,x_E
$$

## 5. Constraints

**(C1) Hire at most 3 employees:**
$$
x_A + x_B + x_C + x_D + x_E \leq 3
$$

**(C2) Total salary within budget of $35,000:**
$$
8100\,x_A + 20000\,x_B + 21000\,x_C + 3000\,x_D + 8000\,x_E \leq 35000
$$

**(C3) At least one Master's or PhD candidate (B or C):**
$$
x_B + x_C \geq 1
$$

**(C4) Total work experience of at least 12 years:**
$$
3\,x_A + 10\,x_B + 4\,x_C + 3\,x_D + 7\,x_E \geq 12
$$

**(C5) At most one of A or E (similar skills):**
$$
x_A + x_E \leq 1
$$

**(C6) Hire at least 2 employees:**
$$
x_A + x_B + x_C + x_D + x_E \geq 2
$$

**(C7) Binary (integrality) constraints:**
$$
x_i \in \{0, 1\}, \quad \forall i \in \{A, B, C, D, E\}
$$

## 6. Complete Compact Form

$$
\begin{aligned}
\min \quad & \sum_{i \in I} s_i \, x_i \\[4pt]
\text{s.t.} \quad & 2 \leq \sum_{i \in I} x_i \leq 3 \\
& \sum_{i \in I} s_i \, x_i \leq 35000 \\
& x_B + x_C \geq 1 \\
& \sum_{i \in I} e_i \, x_i \geq 12 \\
& x_A + x_E \leq 1 \\
& x_i \in \{0, 1\}, \quad \forall i \in I
\end{aligned}
$$

## 7. Expected Optimal Solution

Solving this MILP yields the optimal solution:
$$
x_B^* = 1, \quad x_D^* = 1, \quad x_A^* = x_C^* = x_E^* = 0
$$

**Optimal objective value:** $Z^* = 20000 + 3000 = \$23{,}000$

**Verification of constraints:**
- Team size: 2 employees (within [2, 3]) ✓
- Budget: $23{,}000 \leq \$35{,}000$ ✓
- Education: B (Master's) is hired ✓
- Experience: $10 + 3 = 13 \geq 12$ years ✓
- A/E conflict: only D and B are hired, neither A nor E ✓

# MILP Formulation: Employee Hiring Optimization

## Decision Variables

For each candidate $i \in \{A, B, C, D, E\}$, define a binary variable:

$$
x_i = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if candidate } i \text{ is hired} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
$$

So we have $x_A, x_B, x_C, x_D, x_E \in \{0, 1\}$.

## Objective Function

Minimize the total salary paid to the selected candidates:

$$
\min Z = 8100\,x_A + 20000\,x_B + 21000\,x_C + 3000\,x_D + 8000\,x_E
$$

## Constraints

**(1) Team size — between 2 and 3 employees:**

$$
2 \le x_A + x_B + x_C + x_D + x_E \le 3
$$

**(2) Budget limit of $35,000:**

$$
8100\,x_A + 20000\,x_B + 21000\,x_C + 3000\,x_D + 8000\,x_E \le 35000
$$

**(3) At least one Master's or PhD candidate** (only B and C qualify):

$$
x_B + x_C \ge 1
$$

**(4) Minimum total work experience of 12 years:**

$$
3\,x_A + 10\,x_B + 4\,x_C + 3\,x_D + 7\,x_E \ge 12
$$

**(5) At most one of A and E** (similar professional skills):

$$
x_A + x_E \le 1
$$

**(6) Binary restrictions:**

$$
x_A, x_B, x_C, x_D, x_E \in \{0, 1\}
$$

## Complete Model

$$
\begin{aligned}
\min \quad & Z = 8100\,x_A + 20000\,x_B + 21000\,x_C + 3000\,x_D + 8000\,x_E \\[2mm]
\text{s.t.} \quad & 2 \le x_A + x_B + x_C + x_D + x_E \le 3 \\
& 8100\,x_A + 20000\,x_B + 21000\,x_C + 3000\,x_D + 8000\,x_E \le 35000 \\
& x_B + x_C \ge 1 \\
& 3\,x_A + 10\,x_B + 4\,x_C + 3\,x_D + 7\,x_E \ge 12 \\
& x_A + x_E \le 1 \\
& x_i \in \{0,1\}, \quad \forall i \in \{A,B,C,D,E\}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Explanation of Model Elements

| Element | Meaning |
|---------|---------|
| **Variables $x_i$** | Binary hire/no-hire decisions — the source of integrality (MILP, not LP). |
| **Objective** | Linear in $x_i$ with salary coefficients; minimization drives selection toward the cheapest feasible team. |
| **Constraint (1)** | Combined bound on team size: hire between 2 and 3 candidates. |
| **Constraint (2)** | Knapsack-style budget cap using the same salary coefficients as the objective. |
| **Constraint (3)** | Logical "OR" — at least one of the two highly-educated candidates (B or C) must be chosen. |
| **Constraint (4)** | Covering constraint ensuring the team accumulates at least 12 years of experience. |
| **Constraint (5)** | Mutual-exclusion constraint preventing both A and E from being hired together. |
| **Constraint (6)** | Forces integrality — without it, fractional hires would be allowed. |

## Optimal Solution

Solving the model yields:

$$
x_B = 1, \quad x_D = 1, \quad x_A = x_C = x_E = 0
$$

- **Total cost:** $Z^* = 20{,}000 + 3{,}000 = \$23{,}000$
- **Team size:** 2 ✓
- **Budget:** $\$23{,}000 \le \$35{,}000$ ✓
- **Master's/PhD:** Candidate B has a Master's degree ✓
- **Experience:** $10 + 3 = 13 \ge 12$ years ✓
- **A/E rule:** $0 + 0 = 0 \le 1$ ✓

# Workforce Planning MILP — Best Model

## 1. Sets and Data

$$T = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$$

**Initial conditions:** $W_0 = 40$, $I_0 = 0$

**Demand:** $(d_1, d_2, d_3, d_4, d_5, d_6) = (700, 600, 500, 800, 900, 800)$

**Cost parameters:**
- Overtime: $c_o = 5$ €/unit
- Holding: $c_h = 10$ €/unit/month
- Hiring: $c_H = 500$ €/worker
- Layoff: $c_F = 700$ €/worker

**Capacity parameters:**
- Regular production: $p = 20$ units/worker/month
- Overtime cap: $p_e = 6$ units/worker/month
- Hiring/layoff limit: $\Delta = 5$ workers/month

## 2. Decision Variables

| Variable | Meaning | Domain |
|---|---|---|
| $W_t$ | Workers employed in month $t$ | $\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ |
| $H_t$ | Workers hired at start of month $t$ | $\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ |
| $F_t$ | Workers laid off at start of month $t$ | $\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ |
| $O_t$ | Overtime units produced in month $t$ | $\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ |
| $I_t$ | Ending inventory in month $t$ | $\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ |
| $S_t$ | Units sold in month $t$ | $\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ |

## 3. Objective Function

Since revenue $p \cdot \sum_t d_t = 4300p$ is fixed (all demand must be met), maximizing profit is equivalent to **minimizing total operating cost**:

$$\boxed{\min Z = \sum_{t=1}^{6} \left( 5\,O_t + 10\,I_t + 500\,H_t + 700\,F_t \right)}$$

## 4. Constraints

**Workforce balance:**
$$W_t - W_{t-1} - H_t + F_t = 0 \qquad \forall t \in T$$

**Hiring/layoff limits:**
$$0 \leq H_t \leq 5, \quad 0 \leq F_t \leq 5 \qquad \forall t \in T$$

**Overtime capacity:**
$$O_t \leq 6\,W_t \qquad \forall t \in T$$

**Inventory balance:**
$$I_t - I_{t-1} - 20\,W_t - O_t + S_t = 0 \qquad \forall t \in T$$

**Demand satisfaction (all demand must be met):**
$$S_t = d_t \qquad \forall t \in T$$

**Final warehouse condition:**
$$I_6 = 0$$

**Integrality:**
$$W_t, H_t, F_t, O_t, I_t, S_t \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} \qquad \forall t \in T$$

## 5. Compact MILP

$$
\begin{aligned}
\min \quad & \sum_{t=1}^{6} (5O_t + 10I_t + 500H_t + 700F_t) \\
\text{s.t.} \quad & W_t - W_{t-1} - H_t + F_t = 0 && \forall t \\
& 0 \leq H_t \leq 5 && \forall t \\
& 0 \leq F_t \leq 5 && \forall t \\
& O_t \leq 6W_t && \forall t \\
& I_t - I_{t-1} - 20W_t - O_t + d_t = 0 && \forall t \\
& I_6 = 0 \\
& W_0 = 40,\ I_0 = 0 \\
& W_t, H_t, F_t, O_t, I_t \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} && \forall t
\end{aligned}
$$

## 6. LP Relaxation and Integrality Gap

When all variables are relaxed to continuous ($W_t, H_t, F_t, O_t, I_t \in \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$), every integer-feasible solution remains feasible, so:

$$\boxed{Z_{\text{LP}} \leq Z_{\text{MILP}}}$$

- **Absolute integrality gap:** $\Delta_{\text{abs}} = Z_{\text{MILP}} - Z_{\text{LP}}$
- **Relative integrality gap:** $\Delta_{\text{rel}} = \dfrac{Z_{\text{MILP}} - Z_{\text{LP}}}{|Z_{\text{MILP}}|} \times 100\%$

The LP relaxation typically allows fractional hires/layoffs and fractional overtime, which can reduce costs by smoothing the workforce trajectory. The gap measures the cost of forcing integer workforce decisions.

## 7. COPTPY Implementation Sketch

```python
from coptpy import *

env = Envr()
model = env.createModel(name="workforce")

T = range(1, 7)
d = {1:700, 2:600, 3:500, 4:800, 5:900, 6:800}

W = model.addVars(T, vtype=COPT.INTEGER, lb=0, nameprefix="W")
H = model.addVars(T, vtype=COPT.INTEGER, lb=0, ub=5, nameprefix="H")
F = model.addVars(T, vtype=COPT.INTEGER, lb=0, ub=5, nameprefix="F")
O = model.addVars(T, vtype=COPT.INTEGER, lb=0, nameprefix="O")
I = model.addVars(T, vtype=COPT.INTEGER, lb=0, nameprefix="I")

# Workforce balance
model.addConstrs((W[t] - (40 if t==1 else W[t-1]) - H[t] + F[t] == 0
                  for t in T), nameprefix="wf")

# Overtime capacity
model.addConstrs((O[t] <= 6*W[t] for t in T), nameprefix="ot")

# Inventory balance
prev_I = 0
for t in T:
    model.addConstr(I[t] == prev_I + 20*W[t] + O[t] - d[t], nameprefix=f"inv{t}")
    prev_I = I[t]

# Final inventory
model.addConstr(I[6] == 0, name="end_inv")

# Objective
model.setObjective(sum(5*O[t] + 10*I[t] + 500*H[t] + 700*F[t] for t in T),
                   sense=COPT.MINIMIZE)

model.solve()
print("MILP cost:", model.objval)
for t in T:
    print(f"t={t}: W={int(W[t].x)}, H={int(H[t].x)}, F={int(F[t].x)}, "
          f"O={int(O[t].x)}, I={int(I[t].x)}")

# LP relaxation: change vtype=COPT.CONTINUOUS for all variables, re-solve
```

## 8. Assumptions Made

1. **Constant selling price** — revenue is fixed, so maximizing profit = minimizing cost.
2. **No backlogging or lost sales** — all demand must be met each month.
3. **Hiring and layoffs occur at the start of the month** and immediately affect production.
4. **No simultaneous hire-and-fire in the same month** (implicitly optimal since both costs are positive).
5. **No regular-time production cost** — only overtime, holding, hiring, and layoff are penalized.
6. **Inventory measured at end of month** after production and sales.

## Selected Model (Model 2 — most complete formulation)

# MILP: Zhang Family Restaurant Investment Selection

## 1. Sets and Parameters

**Set of candidate restaurants:** $I = \{A, B, C, D\}$

| Restaurant $i$ | Annual income $c_i$ (USD) | Purchase cost $p_i$ (million USD) |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| A | 15,000 | 1.6 |
| B | 40,000 | 2.5 |
| C | 30,000 | 1.8 |
| D | 50,000 | 3.0 |

**Budget:** $B = 6.0$ million USD
**Mutually exclusive pair:** $\{A, D\}$ (if D is bought, A cannot be bought)

## 2. Decision Variables

$$
x_i \in \{0,1\}, \qquad \forall i \in \{A,B,C,D\}
$$

where $x_i = 1$ if restaurant $i$ is purchased and $x_i = 0$ otherwise. The binary domain enforces that each restaurant can be purchased **at most once**.

## 3. Objective Function — maximize total annual income

$$
\max \; Z = 15{,}000\,x_A + 40{,}000\,x_B + 30{,}000\,x_C + 50{,}000\,x_D
$$

*(Equivalently, in \$ thousands: $\max Z = 15x_A + 40x_B + 30x_C + 50x_D$.)*

## 4. Constraints

**(C1) Investment budget** (costs in millions of dollars):
$$
1.6\,x_A + 2.5\,x_B + 1.8\,x_C + 3.0\,x_D \;\le\; 6.0
$$

**(C2) Incompatibility of A and D:**
$$
x_A + x_D \;\le\; 1
$$

**(C3) Binary purchase decisions:**
$$
x_A,\; x_B,\; x_C,\; x_D \;\in\; \{0,1\}
$$

## 5. Complete Compact Form

$$
\begin{aligned}
\max \quad & 15{,}000\,x_A + 40{,}000\,x_B + 30{,}000\,x_C + 50{,}000\,x_D \\[4pt]
\text{s.t.}\quad & 1.6\,x_A + 2.5\,x_B + 1.8\,x_C + 3.0\,x_D \le 6.0 \\[3pt]
& x_A + x_D \le 1 \\[3pt]
& x_A,\,x_B,\,x_C,\,x_D \in \{0,1\}
\end{aligned}
$$

## 6. Assumptions

1. **Atomic purchases** — a restaurant is either bought in full or not at all; partial ownership is not allowed.
2. **One-time purchase** — the $x_i$ variables represent the acquisition decision; income and cost are understood on an annual basis, and the budget is a one-time capital budget.
3. **No interaction effects on income** — total income is additive across purchased restaurants (no synergies or cannibalization).
4. **Budget is the only capital limit** — no minimum-investment, borrowing, or cash-on-hand constraints are imposed beyond the \$6.0 M cap.
5. **The A–D conflict is one-directional in effect but modeled symmetrically** — $x_A + x_D \le 1$ forbids buying D while buying A, which is exactly the stated rule (it also forbids A while buying D; this is the standard reading of the restriction and is not binding at the optimum, since D is purchased and A is not).
6. **No minimum number of restaurants** — buying none would be allowed but is clearly dominated by any positive plan.

## 7. Solution by Enumeration

Only $2^4 = 16$ combinations exist; feasible ones (satisfying C1 and C2):

| Combination | Cost (M\$) | Income ($) | Feasible? |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| $\{\}$ | 0.0 | 0 | ✓ |
| $\{A\}$ | 1.6 | 15,000 | ✓ |
| $\{B\}$ | 2.5 | 40,000 | ✓ |
| $\{C\}$ | 1.8 | 30,000 | ✓ |
| $\{D\}$ | 3.0 | 50,000 | ✓ |
| $\{A,B\}$ | 4.1 | 55,000 | ✓ |
| $\{A,C\}$ | 3.4 | 45,000 | ✓ |
| $\{B,C\}$ | 4.3 | 70,000 | ✓ |
| $\{C,D\}$ | 4.8 | 80,000 | ✓ |
| $\{A,B,C\}$ | 5.9 | 85,000 | ✓ |
| **$\{B,D\}$** | **5.5** | **90,000** | **✓ ★** |
| $\{A,D\},\ \{A,B,D\},\ \{A,C,D\}$ | — | — | ✗ (C2) |
| $\{B,C,D\}$ | 7.3 | — | ✗ (C1) |
| $\{A,B,C,D\}$ | — | — | ✗ (C1, C2) |

## 8. Optimal Solution

$$
\boxed{x_A^* = 0,\quad x_B^* = 1,\quad x_C^* = 0,\quad x_D^* = 1}
\qquad\boxed{Z^* = \$90{,}000 \text{ per year}}
$$

**The Zhang family should purchase Restaurants B and D**, and skip A and C.

## 9. Verification

- **Budget (C1):** $1.6(0) + 2.5(1) + 1.8(0) + 3.0(1) = 5.5 \le 6.0$ ✓ — \$5.5 M spent, \$0.5 M unused.
- **Incompatibility (C2):** $x_A + x_D = 0 + 1 = 1 \le 1$ ✓ — D is bought, A is not.
- **Integrality (C3):** all $x_i \in \{0,1\}$ ✓
- **Optimality:** With D purchased, A is excluded and the best affordable addition is B (\$90,000). Without D, the best feasible set is $\{A,B,C\}$ at \$85,000 — strictly lower. Hence $\{B,D\}$ is optimal.

# Mixed Integer Linear Programming (MILP) Formulation

## 1. Decision Variables

Let binary variable $x_i \in \{0, 1\}$ indicate whether child $i$ is taken on the trip:

| Variable | Child | Cost ($) |
|----------|-------|----------|
| $x_H$ | Harry | 1,200 |
| $x_{He}$ | Hermione | 1,650 |
| $x_R$ | Ron | 750 |
| $x_F$ | Fred | 800 |
| $x_G$ | George | 800 |
| $x_{Gi}$ | Ginny | 1,500 |

Where $x_i = 1$ if child $i$ is taken, and $x_i = 0$ otherwise.

## 2. Objective Function

Minimize the total cost of the trip:

$$\min Z = 1200x_H + 1650x_{He} + 750x_R + 800x_F + 800x_G + 1500x_{Gi}$$

## 3. Constraints

**Capacity constraint** (maximum 4 children):
$$x_H + x_{He} + x_R + x_F + x_G + x_{Gi} \leq 4$$

**Minimum children constraint** (at least 3 children):
$$x_H + x_{He} + x_R + x_F + x_G + x_{Gi} \geq 3$$

**Ginny must be taken** (youngest child):
$$x_{Gi} = 1$$

**Harry conflicts with Fred** (if Harry is taken, Fred cannot be taken):
$$x_H + x_F \leq 1$$

**Harry conflicts with George** (if Harry is taken, George cannot be taken):
$$x_H + x_G \leq 1$$

**George requires Fred** (if George is taken, Fred must be taken):
$$x_G - x_F \leq 0$$

**George requires Hermione** (if George is taken, Hermione must be taken):
$$x_G - x_{He} \leq 0$$

**Binary constraints**:
$$x_i \in \{0, 1\} \quad \forall i \in \{H, He, R, F, G, Gi\}$$

## 4. Solution

Solving this MILP yields the following optimal solution:

| Child | Decision Variable | Value | Cost ($) |
|-------|-------------------|-------|----------|
| Harry | $x_H$ | 0 | 0 |
| Hermione | $x_{He}$ | 0 | 0 |
| Ron | $x_R$ | 1 | 750 |
| Fred | $x_F$ | 1 | 800 |
| George | $x_G$ | 0 | 0 |
| Ginny | $x_{Gi}$ | 1 | 1,500 |

**Optimal Total Cost: $Z^* = \$3,050$**

**Recommended children to take**: **Ginny, Ron, and Fred**

### Verification of Constraints:
- Total children: $0 + 0 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 1 = 3$ ✓ (satisfies $3 \leq \text{children} \leq 4$)
- Ginny is taken ✓
- Harry not taken, so conflict constraints are trivially satisfied ✓
- George not taken, so requirement constraints are trivially satisfied ✓

### Assumptions:
- Each child has a fixed cost as provided.
- The "conflict" and "requirement" relationships are modeled as logical implications using linear inequalities (standard big-M-free approach for binary variables).
- The family takes exactly 3 or 4 children (between the minimum of 3 and maximum of 4).

# MILP Model — Zhang Family Trip Selection

## 1. Sets and Parameters

**Set of children:**
$$C = \{H, He, R, F, G, Gi\} = \{\text{Harry, Hermione, Ron, Fred, George, Ginny}\}$$

**Cost parameter** $c_i \in \mathbb{R}_+$ = trip cost of taking child $i$:

| Child $i$ | Harry ($H$) | Hermione ($He$) | Ron ($R$) | Fred ($F$) | George ($G$) | Ginny ($Gi$) |
|:--|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| $c_i$ | 1200 | 1650 | 750 | 800 | 800 | 1500 |

**Capacity parameters:**
$$N^{\max} = 4 \quad\text{(maximum children on trip)}, \qquad N^{\min} = 3 \quad\text{(minimum children required)}$$

## 2. Decision Variables

$$x_i \in \{0,1\}, \quad \forall i \in C$$

where $x_i = 1$ if child $i$ is taken on the trip, and $x_i = 0$ otherwise. (6 binary variables)

## 3. Objective Function

**Minimize total trip cost:**

$$\min \; Z = \sum_{i \in C} c_i x_i$$

$$Z = 1200\,x_H + 1650\,x_{He} + 750\,x_R + 800\,x_F + 800\,x_G + 1500\,x_{Gi}$$

## 4. Constraints

**(a) Maximum number of children (capacity):**
$$\sum_{i \in C} x_i = x_H + x_{He} + x_R + x_F + x_G + x_{Gi} \le N^{\max} = 4$$

**(b) Minimum number of children:**
$$\sum_{i \in C} x_i \ge N^{\min} = 3$$

**(c) Ginny is definitely taken:**
$$x_{Gi} = 1$$

**(d) Harry excludes Fred** (mutual incompatibility, big-M free):
$$x_H + x_F \le 1$$

**(e) Harry excludes George** (mutual incompatibility):
$$x_H + x_G \le 1$$

**(f) George implies Fred** (logical implication, $x_G \le x_F$):
$$x_G - x_F \le 0$$

**(g) George implies Hermione** (logical implication, $x_G \le x_{He}$):
$$x_G - x_{He} \le 0$$

**Variable domains:**
$$x_i \in \{0,1\} \quad \forall i \in C$$

## 5. Assumptions

1. **Additive, independent costs.** Total trip cost is the sum of per-child costs; no fixed cost, discounts, or interaction effects in cost.
2. **Binary, all-or-nothing selection.** A child is either on the trip or not; no partial attendance.
3. **The stated logical rules are the only behavioral constraints.** Incompatibilities (Harry–Fred, Harry–George) and implications (George→Fred, George→Hermione) are modeled exactly as given, with no further relationships.
4. **Implications are one-directional.** Taking Fred does not force Harry, and taking Hermione does not force George.
5. **Capacity counts children, not seats weighted by age.** The "maximum 4" bound applies to the number of children; Ginny's mandatory attendance consumes one of those slots.
6. **The lower bound of 3 is a hard requirement** (a family decision), not a soft preference.
7. **Costs are given in dollars and are nonnegative**, so the LP relaxation over $\{0,1\}$ has bounded optimum and the MILP is well-posed; the binary restriction is essential for the logical constraints to be meaningful.

## 6. Optimal Solution

| Child | $x_i$ | Cost |
|:--|:--:|--:|
| Harry | 0 | 0 |
| Hermione | 0 | 0 |
| Ron | 1 | 750 |
| Fred | 1 | 800 |
| George | 0 | 0 |
| Ginny | 1 | 1500 |
| **Total** | **3 children** | **\$3,050** |

**$Z^* = 3050$**, with selected set $\{Ginny, Ron, Fred\}$.

**Verification of optimality:** Ginny is forced (1500) and consumes a slot. Exactly two more children must be chosen (bounds 3–4).
- Any set containing George must also contain Fred *and* Hermione, forcing a 4-child set $\{Gi, G, F, He\}$ at cost $1500+800+800+1650 = 4750 > 3050$.
- Any set containing Harry excludes both Fred and George, forcing Hermione: the cheapest such set $\{Gi, H, R, He\}$ costs $1500+1200+750+1650 = 5100 > 3050$.
- The cheapest remaining pair is Ron + Fred = $750 + 800 = 1550$, giving $1500 + 1550 = 3050$, which satisfies all seven constraints.

## Selected Model: Binary Set-Selection (Knapsack) MILP for the Zhang Family Trip

All candidate models generated were equivalent formulations; the following is the most complete presentation.

---

### 1. Sets, Indices and Parameters

**Index set** of the six children:

$$C = \{\text{Harry},\ \text{Hermione},\ \text{Ron},\ \text{Fred},\ \text{George},\ \text{Ginny}\}$$

**Cost parameters** (dollars to take child $i$):

| Child $i$ | Harry | Hermione | Ron | Fred | George | Ginny |
|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| $c_i$ | 1200 | 1650 | 750 | 800 | 800 | 1500 |

**Cardinality bounds:** $L = 3$ (minimum children), $U = 4$ (maximum children).

---

### 2. Decision Variables

$$x_i \in \{0,1\} \qquad \forall i \in C$$

where $x_i = 1$ if child $i$ is taken on the upcoming trip, and $x_i = 0$ otherwise. (Explicitly: $x_H, x_{Hm}, x_R, x_F, x_{Ge}, x_{Gi}$.)

---

### 3. Objective Function

Minimize the total cost of the children taken:

$$\min \; Z = 1200\,x_H + 1650\,x_{Hm} + 750\,x_R + 800\,x_F + 800\,x_{Ge} + 1500\,x_{Gi}$$

---

### 4. Constraints

**(a) Cardinality bounds — at most 4, at least 3 children:**

$$x_H + x_{Hm} + x_R + x_F + x_{Ge} + x_{Gi} \le 4$$

$$x_H + x_{Hm} + x_R + x_F + x_{Ge} + x_{Gi} \ge 3$$

**(b) Mandatory inclusion — Ginny is definitely taken:**

$$x_{Gi} = 1$$

**(c) Mutual exclusion — Harry cannot be taken with Fred:**

$$x_H + x_F \le 1$$

**(d) Mutual exclusion — Harry cannot be taken with George:**

$$x_H + x_{Ge} \le 1$$

**(e) Implication — if George is taken, Fred must be taken** ($\,x_{Ge} \Rightarrow x_F$):

$$x_{Ge} - x_F \le 0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad x_{Ge} \le x_F$$

**(f) Implication — if George is taken, Hermione must be taken** ($\,x_{Ge} \Rightarrow x_{Hm}$):

$$x_{Ge} - x_{Hm} \le 0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad x_{Ge} \le x_{Hm}$$

**(g) Binary domains:**

$$x_H, x_{Hm}, x_R, x_F, x_{Ge}, x_{Gi} \in \{0,1\}$$

---

### 5. Compact Formulation

$$\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\min \quad & \sum_{i \in C} c_i\, x_i \\
\text{s.t.} \quad & L \le \sum_{i \in C} x_i \le U \qquad (L=3,\; U=4)\\
& x_{Gi} = 1\\
& x_H + x_F \le 1\\
& x_H + x_{Ge} \le 1\\
& x_{Ge} \le x_F\\
& x_{Ge} \le x_{Hm}\\
& x_i \in \{0,1\}, \quad \forall i \in C
\end{aligned}}
\]

---

### 6. Modeling Notes / Assumptions

1. **Cost is all-in and additive** — *Assumption:* the total trip cost equals the sum of individual per-child costs, with no shared/fixed trip cost, discount, or interaction term.
2. **"At least three" is interpreted literally** as a lower bound of 3, and it is combined with the "maximum of 4" rule, so the family takes exactly 3 or 4 children. *Assumption:* no requirement that a 4th child be added if 3 suffices — the objective decides.
3. **Incompatibility rules are symmetric exclusions.** The statement "if the couple takes Harry, they will not take Fred" is modeled as a mutual exclusion ($x_H + x_F \le 1$). *Assumption:* the prohibition is symmetric, i.e., taking Fred likewise precludes Harry — which is the natural reading and is also implied by (e), since George ⇒ Fred and Harry ⇒ ¬George would otherwise make George's requirement vacuous.
4. **Implications are one-directional.** $x_{Ge} \le x_F$ does *not* force Fred to bring George (consistent with the problem text).
5. **Ginny's inclusion is unconditional** ($x_{Gi}=1$), so she always consumes one of the 4 available slots.
6. **Logical linearization principles used:** IMPLICATION $a \Rightarrow b \Rightarrow a - b \le 0$; MUTUAL EXCLUSION $\neg(a \land b) \Rightarrow a + b \le 1$; FIXED TRUE $\Rightarrow x_i = 1$. All constraints are linear, so the model is a pure 0–1 ILP (a special case of a MILP).

---

### 7. Optimal Solution (verification)

Because Ginny is mandatory and 3–4 children are required, 2–3 additional children are needed.

| Candidate feasible set | Cost |
|:--|--:|

Text:
# VRPHTW — Mixed‑Integer Linear Programming Formulation

*(Single depot, homogeneous fleet, hard time windows, capacity‑limited)*

---

## 1. Problem data, sets and parameters

### 1.1 Sets

| Set | Definition | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| $N=\{0,1,\dots ,n\}$ | — | All nodes; node $0$ is the distribution centre (depot) |
| $C=N\setminus\{0\}$ | — | Customer set ($n=100$ in the file `r101.txt`) |
| $V=\{1,2,\dots ,K\}$ | — | Vehicles (fleet size $K$, an upper bound; all vehicles identical) |
| $A=\{(i,j):i,j\in N,\ i\neq j\}$ | — | Set of directed arcs |

### 1.2 Parameters

| Parameter | Meaning | Source in `r101.txt` |
|---|---|---|
| $q_i$ | delivery demand of node $i$ ( $=0$ for depot) | col. 3 |
| $e_i$ | earliest time service may **start** at $i$ (ready time) | col. 4 |
| $l_i$ | latest time service may **start** at $i$ (due date) | col. 5 |
| $p_i$ | service (dwell) time at $i$ ( $=0$ for depot) | col. 6 |
| $c_{ij}$ | travel cost/distance $i\to j$ | computed: $c_{ij}=\sqrt{(x_i-x_j)^2+(y_i-y_j)^2}$ |
| $Q$ | vehicle capacity ( $=230$ in the example) | depot row, col. 3 |
| $H$ | planning horizon $= \max_{i\in C} l_i$ ( $=230$ ) | big‑$M$ for time |
| $M_y$ | big‑$M$ for linking constraints, $M_y=1$ sufficient | — |
| $F$ | (optional) fixed cost per vehicle used | — |

Depot parameters: $q_0=0$, $p_0=0$, $e_0=l_0=0$.

### 1.3 Constants derived from data
For every arc $(i,j)\in A$ the travel time equals the travel cost: $t_{ij}=c_{ij}$ (Euclidean, speed $=1$).

---

## 2. Decision variables

| Symbol | Domain | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| $x_{ij}^{k}$ | $\{0,1\}$ | $=1$ iff vehicle $k$ travels the arc $i\to j$ ($j=0$ ⇒ return to depot) |
| $y_{i}^{k}$ | $\{0,1\}$ | $=1$ iff customer $i$ is served by vehicle $k$ |
| $\tau_{i}^{k}$ | $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ | **service start time** of vehicle $k$ at node $i\in C$ (arrival time if it arrives early and waits) |
| $d^{k}$ | $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ | departure time of vehicle $k$ from the depot |
| $r^{k}$ | $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ | return time of vehicle $k$ to the depot |
| $W_{i}^{k}$ | $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ | load of vehicle $k$ **on the arc entering** node $i$ (residual load after service at $i$) |
| $z^{k}$ | $\{0,1\}$ | $=1$ iff vehicle $k$ is used (optional, for the fixed‑cost term) |

---

## 3. Objective function

**Minimise total travel distance (main objective of the VRPHTW):**

$$
\min \; Z \;=\; \sum_{k\in V}\ \sum_{(i,j)\in A} c_{ij}\,x_{ij}^{k}
\;+\; F\sum_{k\in V} z^{k}
$$

*Assumption A‑1:* the objective is pure travel cost, because with **hard** time windows lateness is forbidden and therefore carries no penalty; the (optional) second term prices the number of vehicles used.

---

## 4. Constraints

### 4.1 Demand satisfaction — each customer served exactly once

$$
\sum_{k\in V} y_{i}^{k} = 1 ,\qquad \forall i\in C
\tag{C1}
$$

### 4.2 Flow conservation and route continuity

*At every customer (a vehicle enters iff it leaves and iff it serves):*

$$
\sum_{\substack{j\in N\\ j\neq i}} x_{ij}^{k} \;-\; \sum_{\substack{j\in N\\ j\neq i}} x_{ji}^{k} \;=\; y_{i}^{k} ,\qquad \forall i\in C,\ \forall k\in V
\tag{C2}
$$

*At the depot (one outgoing arc iff one incoming arc — each vehicle performs at most one closed route):*

$$
\sum_{j\in C} x_{0j}^{k} \;=\; \sum_{j\in C} x_{j0}^{k} ,\qquad \forall k\in V
\tag{C3a}
$$

$$
\sum_{j\in C} x_{0j}^{k} \;\le\; 1 ,\qquad \forall k\in V
\tag{C3b}
$$

### 4.3 Linking $y$ and $x$ (a served customer must be entered and left by the same vehicle)

$$
y_{i}^{k} \;\le\; \sum_{\substack{j\in N\\ j\neq i}} x_{ij}^{k} ,\qquad
y_{i}^{k} \;\le\; \sum_{\substack{j\in N\\ j\neq i}} x_{ji}^{k} ,\qquad \forall i\in C,\ \forall k\in V
\tag{C4}
$$

### 4.4 Capacity (CVRP part)

*Version A (sufficient, monotone delivery):*

$$
\sum_{i\in C} q_{i}\,y_{i}^{k} \;\le\; Q ,\qquad \forall k\in V
\tag{C5a}
$$

*Version B (general arc‑flow formulation, valid also with pickup/transshipment):*

$$
W_{i}^{k} \;=\; q_{i}\,y_{i}^{k} \;+\; \sum_{\substack{j\in N\\ j\neq i}} W_{j}^{k}\,x_{ji}^{k} ,\qquad \forall i\in C,\ \forall k\in V
\tag{C5b}
$$

$$
0 \;\le\; W_{i}^{k} \;\le\; Q\,y_{i}^{k} ,\qquad \forall i\in C,\ \forall k\in V
\tag{C5c}
$$

### 4.5 Hard time windows

*Service may start only inside $[e_i,l_i]$; if the vehicle arrives before $e_i$ it waits (no penalty, no restriction):*

$$
e_{i}\,y_{i}^{k} \;\le\; \tau_{i}^{k} \;\le\; l_{i}\,y_{i}^{k} \;+\; H\,(1-y_{i}^{k}) ,\qquad \forall i\in C,\ \forall k\in V
\tag{C6}
$$

$$
0 \;\le\; d^{k} \;\le\; H ,\qquad 0 \;\le\; r^{k} \;\le\; H ,\qquad \forall k\in V
\tag{C7}
$$

### 4.6 Time propagation along the arcs (travel + service; waiting at $j$ is allowed because $\tau_j^k$ may exceed the arrival time)

*From the depot to the first customer:*

$$
\tau_{j}^{k} \;\ge\; d^{k} + p_{0} + c_{0j} \;-\; H\,(1-x_{0j}^{k}) ,\qquad \forall j\in C,\ \forall k\in V
\tag{C8a}
$$

*Between two customers:*

$$
\tau_{j}^{k} \;\ge\; \tau_{i}^{k} + p_{i} + c_{ij} \;-\; H\,(1-x_{ij}^{k}) ,\qquad \forall i,j\in C,\ i\neq j,\ \forall k\in V
\tag{C8b}
$$

*Return to the depot:*

$$
r^{k} \;\ge\; \tau_{i}^{k} + p_{i} + c_{i0} \;-\; H\,(1-x_{i0}^{k}) ,\qquad \forall i\in C,\ \forall k\in V
\tag{C8c}
$$

*Departure must follow the return of the (possibly) same vehicle — not binding for a single trip, but required if several trips per vehicle are allowed:*

$$
d^{k} \;\ge\; r^{k} - H\,(1 - \textstyle\sum_{j\in C}x_{j0}^{k})
$$

### 4.7 Vehicle‑use indicator

$$
z^{k} \;\ge\; \sum_{j\in C} x_{0j}^{k} ,\qquad \sum_{j\in C}x_{0j}^{k} \;\le\; K\,z^{k} ,\qquad \forall k\in V
\tag{C9}
$$

### 4.8 (Optional) symmetry breaking — reduces the search tree without cutting any feasible solution

$$
y_{i}^{k} \;\ge\; y_{i+1}^{k} \quad \forall i\in\{1,\dots ,n-1\},\ \forall k\in V
\tag{C10a}
$$

$$
d^{k} \;\le\; d^{k+1} ,\qquad \forall k\in V,\ k<K
\tag{C10b}
$$

$$
x_{ij}^{k} + x_{ji}^{k} \;\le\; 1 ,\qquad \forall (i,j)\in A,\ i,j\in C,\ \forall k\in V
\tag{C10c}
$$

### 4.9 (Optional) subtour‑elimination strengthening (integer‑cut based)

$$
\sum_{i\in S} y_{i}^{k} \;\le\; |S|-1 + (|S|-1)\bigl(1-\textstyle\sum_{i\in S} y_{i}^{k}\bigr)
$$

is *not* needed — constraints (C2)–(C3) already forbid subtours; the standard MTZ/flow time constraints (C8) provide the required connectivity.

---

## 5. Complete model summary

$$
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& \sum_{k\in V}\sum_{(i,j)\in A} c_{ij}x_{ij}^{k} + F\sum_{k\in V}z^{k}\\[1mm]
\text{s.t.}& \sum_{k}y_{i}^{k}=1 && \forall i\in C \tag{C1}\\
& \sum_{j\neq i}x_{ij}^{k}-\sum_{j\neq i}x_{ji}^{k}=y_{i}^{k} && \forall i\in C,\ k\in V \tag{C2}\\
& \sum_{j\in C}x_{0j}^{k}=\sum_{j\in C}x_{j0}^{k}\le 1 && \forall k\in V \tag{C3}\\
& y_{i}^{k}\le\sum_{j\neq i}x_{ij}^{k},\quad y_{i}^{k}\le\sum_{j\neq i}x_{ji}^{k} && \forall i\in C,\ k\in V \tag{C4}\\
& \sum_{i\in C}q_{i}y_{i}^{k}\le Q && \forall k\in V \tag{C5}\\
& e_{i}y_{i}^{k}\le\tau_{i}^{k}\le l_{i}y_{i}^{k}+H(1-y_{i}^{k}) && \forall i\in C,\ k\in V \tag{C6}\\
& \tau_{j}^{k}\ge d^{k}+c_{0j}-H(1-x_{0j}^{k}) && \forall j\in C,\ k\in V \tag{C8a}\\
& \tau_{j}^{k}\ge\tau_{i}^{k}+p_{i}+c_{ij}-H(1-x_{ij}^{k}) && \forall i,j\in C,\ k\in V \tag{C8b}\\
& r^{k}\ge\tau_{i}^{k}+p_{i}+c_{i0}-H(1-x_{i0}^{k}) && \forall i\in C,\ k\in V \tag{C8c}\\
& x,y\in\{0,1\},\ \tau,d,r,W\ge 0
\end{aligned}
$$

---

## 6. Explicit assumptions

* **A‑1 (objective)** Travel distance is the only penalised quantity; the optional fixed vehicle cost $F$ may be switched off.
* **A‑2 (fleet)** Homogeneous fleet of $K$ identical vehicles of capacity $Q=230$; $K$ is an upper bound (unlimited‑fleet variant: drop (C3b)/(C9) and keep $F>0$).
* **A‑3 (single depot)** All routes start and end at node $0$; no intermediate depots.
* **A‑4 (hard windows)** Service must *start* in $[e_i,l_i]$; early arrival ⇒ waiting is free and unlimited; late arrival is forbidden (no lateness term, no penalty variables). If "must be served *within* the window" is interpreted as "service must *complete* by $l_i$", replace $e_i y_i^k\le\tau_i^k$ by $e_i y_i^k\le\tau_i^k$ and $l_i y_i^k+H(1-y_i^k)$ by $(l_i-p_i)y_i^k+H(1-y_i^k)$.
* **A‑5 (single visit)** Each customer is served by exactly one vehicle, once; no split deliveries (relax by replacing (C1) with $\sum_k y_i^k\ge1$ and introducing partial loads $q_i\lambda_{ik}$).
* **A‑6 (load monotonicity)** Goods are loaded at the depot only, so the vehicle load decreases along the route ⇒ (C5a) is exact; (C5b–c) is the general alternative.
* **A‑7 (time horizon)** $H=\max_i l_i=230$ is a valid big‑$M$ since all routes must be completed inside the horizon; the depot may be left at any time $d^k\ge0$ (waiting at the depot is free).
* **A‑8 (metric)** Euclidean distances, symmetric travel times, unit speed, no arc capacity limits, no time‑dependent costs.
* **A‑9 (symmetry breaking)** Constraints (C10) are optional valid inequalities; they do not remove optimal solutions.
* **A‑10 (data)** All parameters are integers/rational ⇒ the model is a pure MILP solvable by branch‑and‑cut (the Solomon `r101` instance: $n=100$, $Q=230$, $p_i=10$, $e_i/l_i$ as in the file).

---

## 7. Extensions (for reference)

* **Soft time windows (VRPSTW):** replace (C6) by $\tau_i^k \ge e_i - P^{E}\alpha_i$, $\tau_i^k \le l_i + P^{L}\beta_i$, $\alpha_i,\beta_i\in[0,1]$, and add $P^E\sum\alpha_i+P^L\sum\beta_i$ to the objective.
* **Multiple vehicles per customer / split demand:** replace (C1) and (C5a) with fractional $q_i\lambda_{ik}$, $\sum_k\lambda_{ik}=1$, $\sum_i q_i\lambda_{ik}\le Q$.
* **Solution procedure:** an MILP solver (branch‑and‑cut) with subtour/ time‑window cuts; for $n=100$ a hybrid metaheuristic (e.g. ALNS with a time‑window repair operator) is usually preferred, using this MILP as a benchmark/sub‑problem.

# VRPHTW — Vehicle Routing Problem with Hard Time Windows

### Executive Summary

A single distribution center (depot) at node 0 dispatches a homogeneous fleet of vehicles to serve $n=100$ customers. Each customer $i\in C=\{1,\dots,100\}$ has a demand $q_i$, a **hard** time window $[e_i,l_i]$ within which service must *start*, and a service duration $s_i$. Vehicles may arrive early and wait (free waiting); arriving late is infeasible. Every vehicle departs from and returns to the depot, carries at most $Q$ units, and each customer is served exactly once. The objective is to minimize total travel distance (the classical VRPHTW objective, since delays are forbidden), optionally plus a fixed cost per dispatched vehicle.

---

## 1. Data and Parameter Instantiation

**Input file format (Solomon-style, `r101`):** each line is

$$\underbrace{\text{id}}_{1}\ \ \underbrace{x_i}_{2}\ \ \underbrace{y_i}_{3}\ \ \underbrace{q_i}_{4}\ \ \underbrace{e_i}_{5}\ \ \underbrace{l_i}_{6}\ \ \underbrace{s_i}_{7}$$

**Depot row (node 0):** $\;x_0=35,\; y_0=35,\; q_0=0,\; e_0=0,\; l_0=H=230,\; s_0=0$

**Aggregate statistics for this instance:**

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| $n=\|C\|$ | 100 |
| $D=C\cup\{0\}$ | 101 nodes |
| $\sum_{i\in C} q_i$ | 1721 |
| $K$ (max vehicles) | 25 |
| $Q$ (capacity) | 200 |
| $H$ (horizon / depot due date) | 230 |
| minimum vehicles required $\lceil 1721/200\rceil$ | 9 |
| service times | $s_i\ge 1$ for all $i\in C$ |

**Assumptions (explicit):**
1. **A1** Homogeneous fleet of $K$ identical vehicles, capacity $Q$, each used at most once; a used vehicle performs one closed route $0\to\cdots\to 0$.
2. **A2** Each customer is served exactly once (single visit), fully (no partial deliveries).
3. **A3** Unit speed: travel time between nodes equals distance.
4. **A4** *Hard* time windows: service at $i$ must **start** in $[e_i,l_i]$; early arrival ⇒ free waiting until $e_i$; late arrival is infeasible (no penalty variables).
5. **A5** All vehicles leave the depot at time $0$; all must return by $H=230$; the depot is also a customer of demand 0 with window $[0,230]$.
6. **A6** Distances are Euclidean on the given coordinates, truncated to integers (Solomon convention): $d_{ij}=\lfloor\sqrt{(x_i-x_j)^2+(y_i-y_j)^2}\rfloor$.
7. **A7** Objective = total distance travelled; a fixed per-vehicle cost $c\ge0$ is optional ($c=0$ ⇒ pure distance minimisation).

---

## 2. Sets

$$
\begin{aligned}
C &= \{1,\dots,100\} &&\text{customers}\\
D &= C\cup\{0\} &&\text{nodes, depot } 0\\
V &= \{1,\dots,K\},\quad K=25 &&\text{vehicles}\\
A &= \{(i,j)\in D\times D:\ i\neq j\} &&\text{all arcs}\\
A_1 &= \{(i,j)\in A:\ i\in C,\ e_i+s_i+d_{ij}\le l_j\} &&\text{time-window-feasible customer arcs}\\
A_2 &= \{(i,0)\in A:\ i\in C,\ e_i+s_i+d_{i0}\le H\} &&\text{time-window-feasible return arcs}\\
A_0 &= \{(0,j): j\in C\} &&\text{depot departure arcs}\\
A^{\!*}=A_1\cup A_2\cup A_0 &&\text{arc set used by the model}
\end{aligned}
$$

---

## 3. Parameters

| Symbol | Meaning | Domain |
|---|---|---|
| $q_i$ | demand of customer $i$ | $\mathbb{Z}_+$, $q_0=0$ |
| $e_i,\;l_i$ | earliest / latest service-start time | $\mathbb{Z}_+$, $e_i\le l_i$ |
| $s_i$ | service duration at $i$ | $\mathbb{Z}_+$, $s_0=0$, $s_i\ge1\ (i\in C)$ |
| $d_{ij}$ | travel distance (= travel time) from $i$ to $j$ | $\mathbb{Z}_+$ |
| $Q=200$ | vehicle capacity | $\mathbb{R}_+$ |
| $H=230$ | planning horizon, depot due date | $\mathbb{R}_+$ |
| $c\ge0$ | fixed cost per dispatched vehicle ($c=0$ default) | $\mathbb{R}_+$ |
| $M$ | big‑$M$ for time constraints (valid value: $M=H$) | $\mathbb{R}_+$ |

---

## 4. Decision Variables

| Variable | Domain | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| $x_{ij}$ | $\{0,1\}$, $(i,j)\in A^{\!*}$ | 1 if arc $(i,j)$ is traversed by some vehicle |
| $y_k$ | $\{0,1\}$, $k\in V$ | 1 if vehicle $k$ is dispatched |
| $u_i$ | $[e_i,l_i]$, $i\in D$ | **service start time** at node $i$ ($u_0=0$: depot departure) |
| $f_{ij}$ | $\mathbb{Z}_+$, $(i,j)\in A^{\!*}$ | number of vehicles traversing arc $(i,j)$ |
| $g_{ij}$ | $\mathbb{R}_+$, $(i,j)\in A^{\!*}$ | remaining load carried **on** arc $(i,j)$ |
| $z_{kj}$ | $\{0,1\}$, $k\le R,\ j\in C$ | 1 if customer $j$ is the **first** customer of route $k$ |

with $R=\sum_{k\in V}y_k$ (number of routes/vehicles used).

---

## 5. Objective Function

$$
\boxed{\;\min\; Z \;=\; \sum_{(i,j)\in A^{\!*}} d_{ij}\,x_{ij} \;+\; c\sum_{k\in V} y_k\;}
$$

* $c=0$: pure minimisation of total travel distance (standard VRPHTW objective).
* $c>0$: adds a fixed dispatch cost per vehicle; note the trade-off that $c=0$ may use more vehicles than the minimum needed.

---

## 6. Constraints

### (C1) Customer degree — each customer served exactly once

$$
\sum_{\substack{j\in D\\ j\neq i}} x_{ij}=1,\qquad \forall i\in C
\qquad\qquad
\sum_{\substack{i\in D\\ i\neq j}} x_{ij}=1,\qquad \forall j\in C
\tag{C1}
$$

### (C2) Depot degree — number of routes equals number of used vehicles

$$
\sum_{j\in C} x_{0j}=\sum_{k\in V}y_k,
\qquad\qquad
\sum_{i\in C} x_{i0}=\sum_{k\in V}y_k
\tag{C2}
$$

### (C3) Vehicle-count (route) flow — subtour-elimination certificate and route counting

$$
x_{ij}\le f_{ij}\le K\,x_{ij},\qquad \forall (i,j)\in A^{\!*}
\tag{C3a}
$$

$$
\sum_{\substack{i\in D\\ i\neq j}} f_{ij}-\sum_{\substack{j'\in D\\ j'\neq j}} f_{j'j}=0,\qquad \forall j\in C
\tag{C3b}
$$

$$
\sum_{j\in C}f_{0j}-\sum_{i\in C}f_{i0}=0,
\qquad
\sum_{j\in C}f_{0j}=\sum_{k\in V}y_k
\tag{C3c}
$$

### (C4) Hard time windows

$$
u_0=0
\tag{C4a}
$$

$$
e_i\ \le\ u_i\ \le\ l_i,\qquad \forall i\in D
\tag{C4b}
$$

### (C5) Time propagation along used arcs (MTZ on service times; no big‑$M$ needed on $i\ne0$)

$$
u_j\ \ge\ u_i+s_i+d_{ij}-H\,(1-x_{ij}),\qquad \forall (i,j)\in A^{\!*},\ i\neq 0
\tag{C5a}
$$

$$
u_j\ \ge\ d_{0j}-H\,(1-x_{0j}),\qquad \forall j\in C
\tag{C5b}
$$

$$
u_i+s_i+d_{i0}\ \le\ H-H\,(1-x_{i0}),\qquad \forall i\in C
\tag{C5c}
$$

*(C5c) is implied by (C5a) applied to $(i,0)$ with $u_0=0$, and is retained explicitly for solver strength.*

### (C6) Capacity — delivery-commodity (load) flow

$$
g_{ij}\le Q\,x_{ij},\qquad \forall (i,j)\in A^{\!*}
\tag{C6a}
$$

$$
\sum_{\substack{i\in D\\ i\neq j}} g_{ij}-\sum_{\substack{j'\in D\\ j'\neq j}} g_{j'j}=q_j,\qquad \forall j\in C
\tag{C6b}
$$

$$
\sum_{j\in C}g_{0j}=\sum_{i\in C}q_i=1721,
\qquad
\sum_{j\in C}g_{j0}=0
\tag{C6c}
$$

### (C7) Route canonicalisation / symmetry breaking

$$
z_{kj}\le x_{0j},\qquad
\sum_{j\in C}z_{kj}=1,\qquad
\sum_{k\le R}z_{kj}\le 1,
\tag{C7a}
$$

$$
\sum_{\substack{j\in C\\ j>j'}} z_{kj'}\ \ge\ k,\qquad \forall k=1,\dots,R
\tag{C7b}
$$

$$
y_k\ge y_{k+1},\qquad k=1,\dots,K-1
\tag{C7c}
$$

*(C7b) orders routes by the index of their first customer, removing route-label symmetry; (C7c) removes vehicle-label symmetry.*

---

## 7. Worked Check of the Load Formulation (C6)

Route $0\to a\to b\to 0$ serving customers $a,b$:

| arc | $g$ value |
|---|---|
| $(0,a)$ | $q_a+q_b$ |
| $(a,b)$ | $q_b$ |
| $(b,0)$ | $0$ |

- At $a$: in-flow $g_{0a}=q_a+q_b$, out-flow $g_{ab}=q_b$ ⇒ in − out $=q_a$ ✓ (C6b).
- At $b$: in-flow $g_{ab}=q_b$, out-flow $g_{b0}=0$ ⇒ in − out $=q_b$ ✓ (C6b).
- Depot: $\sum_j g_{0j}=q_a+q_b$ = total demand ✓ (C6c); $\sum_j g_{j0}=0$ ✓.
- Capacity: the load is **non-increasing** along a route ($q_a+q_b \ge q_b \ge 0$), so the binding test is the first arc; (C6a) with $g_{0a}\le Qx_{0a}$ is equivalent to $q_a+q_b\le Q$. Hence (C6) is exact. ✓

---

## 8. Correctness Argument

**(⇒ Feasibility ⇒ routing.)** (C1) forces every customer to have exactly one predecessor and one successor; (C2) gives the depot out-degree = in-degree = $R$. Hence the selected arcs form a disjoint union of $R$ directed paths covering all customers, each closed through the depot — i.e. $R$ vehicle routes. (C3) is a consistent $R$-unit flow on those arcs ($f_{ij}$ = number of routes using $(i,j)$), providing a redundant subtour-elimination certificate.

**(⇒ Subtour elimination is exact.)** Suppose a subtour $i_1\to i_2\to\cdots\to i_m\to i_1$ not containing the depot existed. Summing (C5a) around the cycle and cancelling the $u$'s gives
$$0\ \ge\ \sum_{r=1}^{m}\bigl(s_{i_r}+d_{i_r i_{r+1}}\bigr)\ \ge\ m\cdot 1\ >\ 0,$$
a contradiction (since $s_i\ge1$ for all customers). The depot anchors the time scale through $u_0=0$. **Hence hard time windows make the time-MTZ formulation subtour-free automatically**; (C3) is kept only as a solver-friendly redundant certificate.

**(⇒ Time windows.)** (C4b) enforces $u_i\in[e_i,l_i]$; (C5a)–(C5b) propagate the earliest feasible arrival along each route and permit free waiting (no constraint forces service to begin before $e_j$, and the inequality is one-sided); (C5c) guarantees return to the depot by $H=230$.

**(⇒ Capacity.** See §7: the load flow (C6) reproduces exactly the load carried on each arc, and (C6a) enforces load $\le Q$ on every used arc.

**(⇒ Vehicle count and symmetry.)** (C3c) equates $R=\sum f_{0j}$ with $\sum_k y_k$, so the fleet size is consistent; (C7) removes label symmetry without cutting feasible solutions.

**(⇐ Converse.)** Given any feasible routing plan, set $x_{ij}=1$ on used arcs, $f_{ij}$ = number of routes using $(i,j)$, $g_{ij}$ = actual load on the arc, $u_i$ = actual service-start times (waiting included), $y_k=1$ for dispatched vehicles, $z_{kj}$ for the first customers. All constraints (C1)–(C7) hold, and the objective equals the realised travel distance (plus $c\cdot R$). ∎

---

## 9. Model Size

| Block | Count |
|---|---|
| Binary $x_{ij}$ | $\approx |A^{\!*}|\approx 10{,}000$ |
| Binary $y_k$ | $25$ |
| Binary $z_{kj}$ | $R\cdot n \le 2{,}500$ |
| Continuous $u_i$ | $101$ |
| Continuous $g_{ij}$ | $\approx 10{,}000$ |
| Integer $f_{ij}$ | $\approx 10{,}000$ (integrality may be relaxed) |

---

## 10. Solving Notes

- **Ready for modern MILP solvers** (Gurobi / CPLEX / HiGHS): branch-and-cut on the $x$-binaries with the continuous $u$, $g$ handled by LP propagation.
- **Tighten the big‑$M$:** instead of $M=H$, use per‑arc bounds $M_{ij}=l_j-e_i+s_i+H$, or replace (C5) by **indicator constraints** $\bigl[x_{ij}=1\bigr]\Rightarrow u_j\ge u_i+s_i+d_{ij}$, which avoids big‑$M$ entirely and greatly strengthens the LP relaxation.
- **Strengthening cuts:** capacity cuts $\sum_{i\in S}q_i\le Q\cdot(\text{number of depot arcs into }S)$, time-window cuts on subsets, and the $f$-flow can be tightened with $f_{ij}\le R\,x_{ij}$.
- **Scaling:** for larger fleets or instances, use **branch-and-price** — a set-partitioning master over elementary routes with reduced-cost pricing solved by a labeling algorithm on an extended network carrying resources (time and load); the labeling algorithm simultaneously enforces time windows, capacity, and subtour elimination.
- **Equivalent alternative:** the classical three-index model $x_{ijk}\in\{0,1\}$ with MTZ subtour elimination and big‑$M$ time constraints is mathematically equivalent but far larger and numerically weaker; the two-index formulation above is preferred.

# MILP Model for the Vehicle Routing Problem with Hard Time Windows (VRPHTW)

Below is the selected (and refined) complete linear model, inspired by the Solomon `r101.txt` benchmark instance (100 customers, 25 vehicles, capacity 200, planning horizon 230).

---

## 1. Sets

| Symbol | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| $N = \{0, 1, 2, \ldots, n\}$ | All nodes, where $0$ is the depot |
| $C = N \setminus \{0\}$ | Customers only |
| $K = \{1, 2, \ldots, m\}$ | Available (homogeneous) vehicles |
| $A = \{(i,j) \in N \times N : i \neq j\}$ | Directed arcs |

---

## 2. Parameters

| Symbol | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| $c_{ij}$ | Travel cost on arc $(i,j)$ (Euclidean distance for Solomon) |
| $t_{ij}$ | Travel time on arc $(i,j)$ |
| $d_i$ | Demand of customer $i$, $d_0 = 0$ |
| $Q$ | Vehicle capacity |
| $e_i$ | Earliest service start time at node $i$ |
| $l_i$ | Latest service start time at node $i$ |
| $s_i$ | Service duration at node $i$, $s_0 = 0$ |
| $M_{ij}$ | Big-M constant, e.g., $M_{ij} = l_i + s_i + t_{ij} - e_j$ |

---

## 3. Decision Variables

| Symbol | Type | Description |
|--------|------|-------------|
| $x_{ijk}$ | $\in \{0,1\}$ | $=1$ if vehicle $k$ traverses arc $(i,j)$ |
| $T_{ik}$ | $\geq 0$ | Arrival time of vehicle $k$ at node $i$ |
| $W_{ik}$ | $\geq 0$ | Waiting time of vehicle $k$ at node $i$ |
| $u_{ik}$ | $\geq 0$ | Cumulative load on vehicle $k$ after visiting node $i$ |

---

## 4. Objective Function

Minimize total travel cost:

$$\min \; Z = \sum_{k \in K} \sum_{(i,j) \in A} c_{ij}\, x_{ijk}$$

---

## 5. Constraints

**(C1) Each customer is visited exactly once:**
$$\sum_{k \in K} \sum_{j \in N,\, j \neq i} x_{ijk} = 1 \quad \forall\, i \in C$$

**(C2) Flow conservation at every customer:**
$$\sum_{j \in N,\, j \neq i} x_{ijk} = \sum_{j \in N,\, j \neq i} x_{jik} \quad \forall\, i \in C,\; \forall\, k \in K$$

**(C3) Each vehicle leaves the depot at most once:**
$$\sum_{j \in C} x_{0jk} \leq 1 \quad \forall\, k \in K$$

**(C4) Each vehicle returns to the depot at most once:**
$$\sum_{i \in C} x_{i0k} \leq 1 \quad \forall\, k \in K$$

**(C5) Vehicle capacity bounds:**
$$d_i \leq u_{ik} \leq Q \quad \forall\, i \in C,\; \forall\, k \in K$$
$$u_{0k} = 0 \quad \forall\, k \in K$$

**(C6) MTZ subtour elimination (load propagation):**
$$u_{jk} \geq u_{ik} + d_j - Q\,(1 - x_{ijk}) \quad \forall\, i \in N,\; j \in C,\; i \neq j,\; \forall\, k \in K$$

**(C7) Hard time windows (service must start within window):**
$$e_i \leq T_{ik} + W_{ik} \leq l_i \quad \forall\, i \in N,\; \forall\, k \in K$$

**(C8) Waiting time definition:**
$$W_{ik} \geq e_i - T_{ik} \quad \forall\, i \in N,\; \forall\, k \in K$$
$$W_{ik} \geq 0 \quad \forall\, i \in N,\; \forall\, k \in K$$

**(C9) Arrival time propagation:**
$$T_{jk} \geq T_{ik} + s_i + W_{ik} + t_{ij} - M_{ij}\,(1 - x_{ijk}) \quad \forall\, (i,j) \in A,\; \forall\, k \in K$$

**(C10) Depot departure time:**
$$T_{0k} = 0 \quad \forall\, k \in K$$

---

## 6. Mapping from Solomon `r101.txt` Format

The standard Solomon instance file columns map to model parameters as:

| Solomon Column | Model Parameter |
|----------------|-----------------|
| `CUST NO.` | Node index $i \in N$ |
| `XCOORD`, `YCOORD` | $c_{ij} = t_{ij} = \sqrt{(x_i-x_j)^2 + (y_i-y_j)^2}$ |
| `DEMAND` | $d_i$ |
| `READY TIME` | $e_i$ |
| `DUE DATE` | $l_i$ |
| `SERVICE TIME` | $s_i$ |
| Header `NUMBER` | $m = \|K\| = 25$ |
| Header `CAPACITY` | $Q = 200$ |

For `r101`: $n = 100$, $|N| = 101$, $|K| = 25$, depot time window $[0, 230]$, service time $s_i = 10$ for all customers.

---

## 7. Key Modeling Assumptions

1. **Homogeneous fleet**: All vehicles have identical capacity $Q$.
2. **Hard time windows**: Vehicles may arrive early and wait, but cannot start service after $l_i$.
3. **Single depot**: All routes start and end at node 0.
4. **Split deliveries prohibited**: Each customer is served by exactly one vehicle (constraint C1).
5. **Travel time = distance**: Following Solomon convention, $t_{ij} = c_{ij}$.
6. **Sufficient vehicles**: $|K|$ is large enough that all customers can be served (typically 25 for r101).
7. **Big-M tightness**: Using $M_{ij} = l_i + s_i + t_{ij} - e_j$ strengthens the LP relaxation versus a global $M$.

---

## 8. Explanation of Key Elements

- **$x_{ijk}$**: Three-index routing variables — required because time and load are vehicle-specific.
- **$T_{ik}, W_{ik}$**: Separating arrival and waiting times allows explicit modeling of early arrivals; service begins at $T_{ik} + W_{ik}$.
- **$u_{ik}$ (MTZ)**: Eliminates subtours by forcing cumulative load to increase monotonically along each route.
- **C9**: The big-$M$ term activates the time relationship only when $x_{ijk}=1$.
- **C7 + C8**: Together enforce hard time windows — if a vehicle arrives before $e_i$, it waits ($W_{ik} > 0$); if it would arrive after $l_i$, the route is infeasible.
- **Symmetry**: The model is symmetric in vehicles; lexicographic ordering or fixing the first $|C|$ arcs can accelerate solving.

This formulation is solvable directly by MILP solvers (Gurobi, CPLEX) for small instances, or serves as the master problem in branch-and-price / column-generation methods for larger Solomon benchmarks.

## MILP Model: Mary's Dinner (Fiber Maximization under a Budget)

---

### 1. Sets

| Set | Members | Comment |
|---|---|---|
| $V$ | $\{\text{okra},\text{carrots},\text{celery},\text{cabbage}\}$ | Vegetables |
| $P$ | $\{\text{salmon},\text{beef},\text{pork}\}$ | Protein sources |

### 2. Parameters

**Fiber content (grams of fiber per 100 g of food):**

| $i$ | okra | carrots | celery | cabbage | salmon | beef | pork |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $f_i$ | 3.2 | 2.7 | 1.6 | 2.0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |

**Price ($ per 100 g of food):**

| $i$ | okra | carrots | celery | cabbage | salmon | beef | pork |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $c_i$ | 2.6 | 1.2 | 1.6 | 2.3 | 4.0 | 3.6 | 1.8 |

Other parameters:
- $B = 15$ — budget ($)
- $W = 600$ — total weight of the meal (g)
- $m = 50$ — **minimum portion** of any *selected* food (g) *(assumption)*
- $M = 600$ — big‑$M$ for linking (no single food can exceed the 600 g meal) *(assumption)*

Per-gram coefficients used in the model: fiber $f_i/100$ (e.g. okra $0.032$), price $c_i/100$ (e.g. okra $0.026$).

### 3. Decision Variables

- $x_v \ge 0$: grams of vegetable $v \in V$ purchased (continuous)
- $x_p \ge 0$: grams of protein $p \in P$ purchased (continuous)
- $y_v \in \{0,1\}$: $y_v = 1$ iff vegetable $v$ is purchased
- $z_p \in \{0,1\}$: $z_p = 1$ iff protein $p$ is the chosen protein source

### 4. Objective Function

$$\max \; Z=\sum_{v\in V}\frac{f_v}{100}x_v \;+\;\sum_{p\in P}\frac{f_p}{100}x_p$$

$$\boxed{\max\; Z = 0.032\,x_{\text{okra}} + 0.027\,x_{\text{carrots}} + 0.016\,x_{\text{celery}} + 0.020\,x_{\text{cabbage}}}$$

(Protein contributes no fiber; only the vegetable terms are non-zero.)

### 5. Constraints

**(C1) Total weight of the meal:**
$$\sum_{v\in V} x_v + \sum_{p\in P} x_p = 600$$

**(C2) Budget:**
$$\sum_{v\in V}\frac{c_v}{100}x_v + \sum_{p\in P}\frac{c_p}{100}x_p \;\le\; 15$$
$$0.026x_{\text{okra}}+0.012x_{\text{carrots}}+0.016x_{\text{celery}}+0.023x_{\text{cabbage}}+0.040x_{\text{salmon}}+0.036x_{\text{beef}}+0.018x_{\text{pork}}\le 15$$

**(C3) Exactly one protein source is chosen ("either … or"):**
$$\sum_{p\in P} z_p = 1$$

**(C4) Protein linking (a non-chosen protein buys nothing; a chosen one buys a real portion):**
$$m\,z_p \;\le\; x_p \;\le\; M\,z_p \qquad \forall p\in P$$

**(C5) At least two of the four vegetables are selected:**
$$\sum_{v\in V} y_v \;\ge\; 2$$

**(C6) Vegetable linking (selection ⇔ positive purchase):**
$$m\,y_v \;\le\; x_v \;\le\; M\,y_v \qquad \forall v\in V$$

**(C7) Domains:**
$$x_v, x_p \ge 0,\qquad y_v \in \{0,1\},\; z_p\in\{0,1\}$$

### 6. Assumptions (explicitly flagged)

1. **A1 (divisibility):** Foods may be bought in fractional grams; $x$ are continuous.
2. **A2 (meaningful portions):** A food counted as "selected" must be bought in at least $m=50$ g, otherwise the binary selection variables could be satisfied by a 0‑gram purchase. *(This is a modeling assumption; the problem statement gives no minimum portion.)*
3. **A3 (one protein):** "either salmon, beef or pork" is modelled as exactly one; the protein must be a positive quantity.
4. **A4 (≥2 vegetables):** The two vegetables must be *distinct types* with positive amounts.
5. **A5 (no fiber from meat):** Animal protein contributes 0 g fiber.
6. **A6 (leftover money allowed):** The budget is an inequality; unused money is permitted.
7. **A7 (exact weight):** Total intake is exactly 600 g.
8. **A8 (big‑M):** $M=600$ g is valid because no single item can exceed the 600 g meal.

### 7. Optimal Solution (with $m = 50$ g)

| Food | Grams | Fiber (g) | Cost ($) | Selected |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Okra | **500** | 16.00 | 13.00 | ✔ |
| Carrots | **50** | 1.35 | 0.60 | ✔ |
| Celery | 0 | 0 | 0 | ✘ |
| Cabbage | 0 | 0 | 0 | ✘ |
| Pork | **50** | 0 | 0.90 | ✔ |
| Salmon / Beef | 0 | 0 | 0 | ✘ |

- Total weight = 600 g ✔, Total cost = **$14.50** ≤ $15 ✔ (slack $0.50)
- **Maximum fiber = 17.35 g**
- Selected: 2 vegetables (okra, carrots) ✔, exactly 1 protein (pork) ✔

**Why this is optimal:** proteins give no fiber, so pork (cheapest, $0.018/g) is chosen to protect the budget (salmon/beef at the same weights would break $B$); among vegetables okra has the highest fiber per gram (0.032), so with the weight fixed at 600 g the fiber is maximized by putting as much weight as possible into okra while keeping the minimum required portions of a second vegetable and of the protein.

**Sensitivity to assumption A2** (minimum portion $m$):

| $m$ | Optimal purchase | Fiber (g) | Cost ($) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 50 g | okra 500, carrots 50, pork 50 | 17.35 | 14.50 |
| 100 g (whole 100‑g portions) | okra 400, carrots 100, pork 100 | 15.50 | 13.40 |
| $m \to 0$ (degenerate) | okra ≈ 557, carrots ≈ 43, pork ≈ 0 | ≈ 18.99 | 15.00 |

## Best Model (selected from 8 candidates — all converged to the same formulation and solution)

### 1. Sets

- Vegetables: \(V=\{\text{okra, carrots, celery, cabbage}\}\)
- Proteins: \(P=\{\text{salmon, beef, pork}\}\)
- All items: \(I=V\cup P\)

### 2. Parameters

Fiber \(f_i\) (g per 100 g) and price \(c_i\) (\$ per 100 g):

| Item \(i\) | \(f_i\) | \(c_i\) |
|---|---:|---:|
| Okra | 3.2 | 2.60 |
| Carrots | 2.7 | 1.20 |
| Celery | 1.6 | 1.60 |
| Cabbage | 2.0 | 2.30 |
| Salmon | 0 | 4.00 |
| Beef | 0 | 3.60 |
| Pork | 0 | 1.80 |

Meal size \(G=600\) g \(=6\) units of 100 g; budget \(B=\$15\); minimum portion \(m=1\) unit (100 g); minimum vegetable count \(K=2\).

### 3. Variables

- \(q_i\ge 0\): quantity of item \(i\) purchased, **in units of 100 g** (\(q_i=1\) ⇒ 100 g)
- \(y_i\in\{0,1\}\): 1 if item \(i\) is purchased, 0 otherwise

### 4. Objective — maximize fiber intake

\[
\max \; Z=3.2\,q_{\text{okra}}+2.7\,q_{\text{carrots}}+1.6\,q_{\text{celery}}+2.0\,q_{\text{cabbage}}
\]

(Proteins carry no fiber per the data, so their quantities do not appear in the objective.)

### 5. Constraints

**(a) Total intake = 600 g:**
\[
q_{\text{okra}}+q_{\text{carrots}}+q_{\text{celery}}+q_{\text{cabbage}}+q_{\text{salmon}}+q_{\text{beef}}+q_{\text{pork}}=6
\]

**(b) Budget ≤ \$15:**
\[
2.6q_{\text{okra}}+1.2q_{\text{carrots}}+1.6q_{\text{celery}}+2.3q_{\text{cabbage}}+4.0q_{\text{salmon}}+3.6q_{\text{beef}}+1.8q_{\text{pork}}\le 15
\]

**(c) At least two distinct vegetables:**
\[
y_{\text{okra}}+y_{\text{carrots}}+y_{\text{celery}}+y_{\text{cabbage}}\ge 2
\]

**(d) Exactly one protein source:**
\[
y_{\text{salmon}}+y_{\text{beef}}+y_{\text{pork}}=1
\]

**(e) Linking (selection ↔ quantity), for all \(i\in I\):**
\[
q_i\le 6\,y_i \qquad\forall i\in I \quad\text{(if }y_i=0\Rightarrow q_i=0\text{)}
\]
\[
q_i\ge 1\,y_i \qquad\forall i\in I \quad\text{(if }y_i=1\Rightarrow q_i\ge1\text{, i.e. }\ge100\text{ g)}
\]
\(M=6\) is valid because no single item can exceed the 600 g meal.

**(f) Domains:** \(q_i\ge0,\; y_i\in\{0,1\}\).

### 6. Assumptions (marked, as data were incomplete)
1. **Minimum meaningful portion:** a selected item must be bought in ≥ 100 g portions (otherwise "selecting" a vegetable would be meaningless). *This is the key assumption driving the answer.*
2. **Protein fiber = 0** (not specified in the data), so protein contributes nothing to the objective and only displaces vegetables.
3. **Budget is an upper bound** (≤ \$15); total intake is **exactly** 600 g.
4. Purchased grams = consumed grams; quantities are continuous and divisible within the 100 g unit.

### 7. Optimal solution

| Variable | Value | Grams |
|---|---|---|
| \(q_{\text{okra}}\) | 4 | 400 g |
| \(q_{\text{carrots}}\) | 1 | 100 g |
| \(q_{\text{pork}}\) | 1 | 100 g |
| \(q_{\text{celery}}, q_{\text{cabbage}}, q_{\text{salmon}}, q_{\text{beef}}\) | 0 | — |

**Verification:** total \(=400+100+100=600\) g ✓; cost \(=4(2.60)+1(1.20)+1(1.80)=\$13.40\le \$15\) ✓; two vegetables selected ✓; exactly one protein (pork, the cheapest at \$1.80/100 g) ✓.

**Maximum fiber: \(Z^*=4(3.2)+1(2.7)=15.5\) grams.**

*Why this is optimal:* with one 100 g protein portion fixed (pork is cheapest, \$1.8), 5 vegetable units remain. Okra has the highest fiber per unit (3.2), but the "at least two vegetables" rule forces ≥1 unit of a second vegetable; carrots are the best such second vegetable (2.7 vs. cabbage 2.0, celery 1.6). Hence okra 4 units + carrots 1 unit; any shift (e.g. 3 okra + 2 carrots = 15.0 g) is worse, and the budget is non-binding at \$13.40.

Text:
## 1. Interpretation and Assumptions

**Time axis.** The investor starts at the beginning of Year 1 with $W_0 = 100{,}000$ yuan. The horizon ends at the end of Year 3. Index $t=0,1,2$ denotes "the beginning of Year $t+1$"; the terminal moment is the end of Year 3.

**The two options (return conventions).**

* **Type 1 (1‑year option):** 1 yuan invested at the beginning of Year $t+1$ returns **1.7 yuan** at the end of Year $t+1$ (i.e. profit 0.7 yuan per yuan). It may be repeated in every year.
* **Type 2 (2‑year option):** 1 yuan invested at the beginning of Year $t+1$ returns **3.0 yuan** at the end of Year $t+2$ (profit 2 yuan per yuan). Because "the investment time must be a multiple of two years", the money can only be withdrawn after a whole 2‑year block, and a block may only be *started* if it fits completely inside the 3‑year horizon.

**Assumptions (marked, since the statement leaves them open).**

* **A1 (reinvestment).** Money received at the end of a year may be re‑invested in a later year, or simply held idle (idle cash earns 0). This is the natural reading of "maximize the money earned by the third year".
* **A2 (horizon for Type 2).** A 2‑year block may start at the beginning of Year 1 (ends end of Year 2) or at the beginning of Year 2 (ends end of Year 3); a block starting at the beginning of Year 3 would end at the end of Year 4, outside the horizon, so it is **not** allowed (this is where the "multiple of two years" rule bites).
* **A3 (integrality).** If the amounts must be whole yuan, the variables are restricted to non‑negative integers and the model becomes a MILP; the optimal value below is unchanged.

---

## 2. Sets, parameters, variables

**Sets:** $T=\{0,1,2\}$ (beginning of Years 1,2,3); $T_2=\{0,1\}$ (legal starting times of the 2‑year block).

**Parameters:**
$$R_1=1.7 \ \text{(cash per yuan after 1 year)},\qquad R_2=3.0 \ \text{(cash per yuan after 2 years)},\qquad W_0=100{,}000 .$$

**Decision variables** (all $\ge 0$; integer if A3 is imposed):

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $x_t,\ t\in T$ | yuan invested in the **1‑year option** at the beginning of Year $t+1$ (matures end of Year $t+1$) |
| $y_t,\ t\in T_2$ | yuan invested in the **2‑year option** at the beginning of Year $t+1$ (matures end of Year $t+2$) |
| $c_t,\ t\in T$ | idle cash held at the end of Year $t+1$ (no interest) |
| $Z$ | total wealth owned at the **end of Year 3** |

There is no variable $y_2$: the 2‑year block cannot start in Year 3 (A2).

---

## 3. Objective function

$$\max\; Z$$

with $Z$ defined by the terminal cash‑flow equation below. (Equivalently, maximising the *earned profit* $Z-W_0$ gives the identical optimum; see §5 for the equivalent reduced objective.)

---

## 4. Constraints

**(B0) Allocation of the initial capital (end of Year 0 / beginning of Year 1):**
$$x_0+y_0+c_0 = W_0 = 100{,}000$$

**(B1) Cash balance at the end of Year 1** (in: $1.7x_0$ matures + $c_0$ carried over; out: new investments + cash kept):
$$1.7\,x_0+c_0 = x_1+y_1+c_1$$

**(B2) Cash balance at the end of Year 2** (in: $1.7x_1$ from the 1‑year option and $3y_0$ from the 2‑year block both mature; out: 1‑year investment started in Year 3 + cash kept):
$$1.7\,x_1+3\,y_0+c_1 = x_2+c_2$$

**(D) Terminal wealth at the end of Year 3** (in: $1.7x_2$ from the 1‑year option of Year 3 and $3y_1$ from the 2‑year block started in Year 2; plus $c_2$):
$$Z = 1.7\,x_2+3\,y_1+c_2$$

**(N) Bounds / integrality:**
$$x_t\ge 0\ (t\in T),\qquad y_t\ge 0\ (t\in T_2),\qquad c_t\ge 0\ (t\in T),\qquad Z\ge 0$$
$$x_t,\;y_t,\;c_t \in \mathbb{Z}_+ \quad\text{(if A3 is imposed)}$$

*(No additional constraint is needed for the 2‑year rule: it is enforced by the index set $T_2=\{0,1\}$ and by the maturity dates used in (B1)–(B2), (D).)*

---

## 5. Solution

**Optimal value:**
$$\boxed{Z^{*}=510{,}000\ \text{yuan}\quad(\text{profit } 410{,}000\ \text{yuan})}$$

**Optimal strategy.** Let $a$ be any number with $0\le a\le 100{,}000$. An entire family of optimal solutions is:

$$x_0=a,\quad y_0=100{,}000-a,\quad c_0=0$$
$$x_1=0,\quad y_1=1.7\,a,\quad c_1=0$$
$$x_2=3\,(100{,}000-a),\quad c_2=0,\qquad Z=510{,}000 .$$

Two clean representative solutions (endpoints of this family):

* **(A) Long first, short last:** Invest all $100{,}000$ in the **2‑year option** over Years 1–2 → $300{,}000$ at the end of Year 2 → invest all $300{,}000$ in the **1‑year option** in Year 3 → $1.7\times300{,}000 = 510{,}000$ at the end of Year 3.
* **(B) Short first, long last:** Invest all $100{,}000$ in the **1‑year option** in Year 1 → $170{,}000$ at the end of Year 1 → invest all $170{,}000$ in the **2‑year option** over Years 2–3 → $3\times170{,}000 = 510{,}000$ at the end of Year 3.

**Why this is optimal.** Eliminating $c_0,c_1,c_2$ from the constraints gives the equivalent objective

$$Z = 100{,}000+\underbrace{0.7(x_0+x_1+x_2)}_{\text{profit of 1‑year options}}+\underbrace{2(y_0+y_1)}_{\text{profit of 2‑year blocks}} .$$

The per‑yuan profit rates are $0.7$ per year for Type 1 and $2$ per 2‑year block $=1$ per year for Type 2, so Type 2 is the better use of money over a 2‑year horizon — but a 2‑year block must be placed either in Years 1–2 (then the proceeds earn $0.7$ once more in Year 3) or in Years 2–3 (then it is fed by the $0.7$-profit Year‑1 money). Either way the chain yields $0.7+2=2.7$ profit per yuan over the three years, i.e. $5.1\times100{,}000$, and the constraints forbid doing better:

* all‑Type‑1 gives $100{,}000\cdot1.7^3 = 491{,}300 < 510{,}000$;
* a 2‑year block started in Year 3 is infeasible (A2);
* holding idle cash ($c_t>0$) only destroys profit.

Hence $Z^{*}=510{,}000$ and the degenerate family above is optimal.

**Remark on the alternative reading.** If reinvestment of matured money were forbidden (A1 dropped), the model would collapse to $\max\{1.7\sum x_t+3\sum y_t:\ \sum x_t+\sum y_t\le 100{,}000\}$, whose optimum is to put everything into the 2‑year block, giving $300{,}000$ at the end of Year 3. The LP above is the correct formulation under the standard assumption A1.
